title: UI Design Fundamentals
description: Turn your ideas into interfaces people love. Learn visual hierarchy, color, and layout through practical exercises.

lessons.title: Start with visual hierarchy
lessons.body:
Visual hierarchy helps people understand what matters first. Give your primary heading the most emphasis, group related content with spacing, and make one main action clear.

Try it: sketch a sign-up screen. Use size, contrast, and spacing to guide a visitor from the heading to the form and then to the submit button.

lessons.title: Build a thoughtful color palette
lessons.body:
Choose a primary color for key actions, neutral tones for content, and semantic colors for feedback. Check that normal text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background.

Try it: pick a primary color and create three neutral surfaces. Test each text and background pair with a contrast checker.

lessons.title: Create layouts that breathe
lessons.body:
Use a spacing scale such as 4, 8, 16, 24, and 32 pixels. Consistent gaps make a layout feel intentional. Keep reading lines comfortably short and use grids to align related elements.

Try it: design a course card at mobile and desktop widths. Keep the title, description, and main action easy to scan.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of visual hierarchy?
choices: Use as many colors as possible
Guide attention in order of importance
Make every element the same size

quiz.question: What is the minimum recommended contrast for normal text?

title: Build Your First Website
description: From a blank page to your first responsive website. Discover HTML, CSS, and the web one small step at a time.

lessons.title: Give your page structure
lessons.body:
HTML describes the meaning of content. Use a header for the introduction, nav for navigation, main for primary content, and footer for supporting links. Headings should follow a logical order.

Try it: write a simple page with one h1, two sections with h2 headings, and a navigation link to each section.

lessons.title: Style with CSS
lessons.body:
CSS controls presentation. A selector chooses elements, and declarations set properties like color, padding, and display. Use classes for reusable styles.

Try it: create a .card class with padding, a border radius, and a background. Apply it to three different sections.

lessons.title: Make it responsive
lessons.body:
Start with a single-column mobile layout. Add a media query when the content has enough room for multiple columns. Flexible grids and max-width prevent content from becoming too wide.

Try it: use display: grid and grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) for a responsive set of cards.

quiz.question: Which element holds the primary page content?
What helps a layout adapt to screen widths?

title: Learn Smarter, Not Harder
description: Build a learning routine that sticks with active recall, focused study sessions, and realistic goals.

lessons.title: Practice active recall
lessons.body:
Retrieving information from memory strengthens learning more than simply rereading it. After a lesson, close your notes and explain the key idea in your own words.

Try it: write three questions about something you learned today. Answer them without looking, then check your answers.

lessons.title: Space your practice
lessons.body:
Reviewing material over multiple days helps you retain it. Revisit a topic after one day, several days, and a week. Spend extra time on concepts you find difficult.

Try it: schedule three short reviews of your most recent lesson over the next week.

lessons.title: Design your study routine
lessons.body:
A useful goal is specific and achievable. Choose a small daily action, attach it to an existing habit, and keep distractions out of reach. Take breaks to maintain focus.

Try it: set a 25-minute timer, put your phone away, and finish one lesson. Write down one thing you learned before taking a break.

title: JavaScript, Step by Step
description: Bring your websites to life with variables, functions, and interactive events.

lessons.title: Variables and values
lessons.body:
Use const for bindings that do not need reassignment and let for bindings that do. JavaScript supports strings, numbers, booleans, objects, and other value types.

Try it: create a const named courseTitle with a string value and a let named completedLessons initialized to 0. Increase completedLessons by one.

lessons.title: Functions that do one thing
lessons.body:
Functions package reusable behavior. Give them meaningful names and pass inputs as parameters. Return values instead of relying on shared mutable state when possible.

Try it: write a function percentage(completed, total) that returns the completion percentage. Handle the case where total is zero.

lessons.title: Listen for events
lessons.body:
Events let code respond to interactions. Use addEventListener in plain JavaScript or event props like onClick in React. Keep event handlers focused and update state to reflect changes.

Try it: make a button that increments a counter and displays the new value on the page.

quiz.question: Which keyword is suitable for a binding that will be reassigned?
How can a function provide an output?
Which React prop handles a button click?

title: Speak with Confidence
description: Find your voice. Practice clear explanations, thoughtful questions, and confident presentations.

lessons.title: Make your message clear
lessons.body:
Start with the one idea you want people to remember. Put the main point first, then support it with a concrete example. Use short sentences and familiar words.

Try it: explain something you learned recently in three sentences. Ask a friend which idea stood out.

lessons.title: Listen before you respond
lessons.body:
Active listening means paying attention to the meaning behind someone’s words. Ask an open question, paraphrase the answer, and check your understanding before adding your own opinion.

Try it: ask a buddy about a challenge they are facing. Summarize what you heard without immediately offering advice.

lessons.title: Prepare a short presentation
lessons.body:
A useful presentation has a clear opening, a small number of supporting points, and a specific conclusion. Practice aloud and time yourself. Leave room to breathe between ideas.

Try it: deliver a two-minute explanation of a favorite topic. Record it, then choose one thing to improve on your next attempt.

quiz.question: What should a clear explanation begin with?
What helps prepare a presentation?
choices: Adding as many points as possible

title: Make Sense of Everyday Data
description: Ask better questions, spot misleading charts, and turn everyday numbers into useful insights.

lessons.title: Start with a useful question
lessons.body:
Data is most helpful when it answers a specific question. Define what you want to know, which observations you need, and how you will measure them.

Try it: ask whether your study routine is consistent. Record the date and minutes studied for one week, using the same unit each day.

lessons.title: Choose the right summary
lessons.body:
The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations. The median is the middle value after sorting. A very large or small observation can pull the mean away from a typical value.

Try it: find the mean and median of 10, 15, 15, 20, and 90. Consider which better represents a typical study session.

lessons.title: Read charts with care
lessons.body:
Check a chart’s axis labels, units, time range, and source before drawing conclusions. A truncated axis can exaggerate differences. A pattern between two measurements does not prove that one causes the other.

Try it: find a chart in a news article and write down one conclusion it supports and one claim it cannot establish.

quiz.question: What should come before collecting data?
Which summary is often less affected by an extreme value?
